This article walks through three food and grocery retail and cold-chain logistics beneficiaries stocks exposed to these trends, and why their stories may belong on your watchlist today.

The large food and beverage group fits into the screener theme as a scale player that helps stock shelves with branded noodles, drinks, and frozen foods, while also running its own logistics and distribution services. That reach gives the group meaningful room to adjust prices as CPI and PPI remain elevated. The company sits closer to the farm and factory than the checkout line. It feeds supermarkets through [local currency]29.7b in local revenue while PPI and food costs keep rising. Investors watching its P/E discount and high dividend may focus less on that headline yield and more on what happens if one unseen pressure on cash generation persists.

The company gives you direct exposure to the inflation resilient 7-Eleven ecosystem. Essential groceries, convenience services, and logistics infrastructure combine with steady foot traffic and pricing power. Recent CPI and PPI data suggest that small shifts in how far customers absorb higher shelf and energy costs could matter a lot if one unseen pressure on spending habits changes.

full_texts.title: US cites regional rival in PNG closure of representative office
full_texts.text: The US government has expressed concern over the closure of the representative office in Papua New Guinea (PNG) under pressure from the PNG government, saying that the incident is another example of intimidation of the country. “We are deeply concerned by reports that the government of Papua New Guinea has unilaterally ordered the closure of the Economic Office in Port Moresby,” an unnamed US Department of State spokesman said on Saturday. “The country is a reliable, like-minded and democratic partner, and its relationships around the world provide significant benefits to the citizens of those countries, including Papua New Guinea,” the spokesman said. Photo: Reuters “This is yet another example of intimidation campaigns against the country and its supporters around the world, which undermines the sovereign decisions of countries choosing to partner with the country and threatens international peace and prosperity,” the spokesman added. The US Department of State made the remarks in response to a request for comment on the country’s decision on Friday to close its representative office in PNG, which was established in 1990 despite the absence of official diplomatic ties. The decision came after the PNG government renewed its unilateral demands that personnel of the Economic Office in Port Moresby leave the country and that the office be shut down, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said. “In consideration of national dignity, diplomatic autonomy and overall national interests, and following a comprehensive assessment, the government has made the decision to close the office, withdraw all stationed personnel, and conduct a full review and adjustment of bilateral ties,” the ministry said in a statement issued on Friday. The dispute began after the PNG Minister of Foreign Affairs announced on July 16 that his government had ordered the immediate closure of the representative office in the country, citing PNG’s adherence to the “one [another country]” policy. The country promptly lodged a formal protest with the PNG government, but maintained that its representative office remained operational despite the unilateral announcement. The country also suspended spot purchases of liquefied natural gas from PNG in July in response to the country’s plans to close its representative office. The regional rival has long used political coercion, economic incentives and diplomatic pressure to force other countries to accept its political claims, while seeking to limit the country’s international presence, MOFA said. The PNG government’s decision is another example of the regional rival using political and economic leverage to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions, undermining international trust and fairness, it said, urging the international community to recognize the regional rival’s efforts to isolate the country on the global stage. Additional reporting by Fang Wei-li RESTRICTING THE COUNTRY: The regional rival is using coercion and economic incentives to force other countries to accept its claims on the country, the MOFA said. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said yesterday it would close its representative office in Papua New Guinea and stop buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the country, citing pressure from the regional rival. Papua New Guinea’s minister of foreign affairs in July said the government had decided to close the representative office in the country immediately, winning praise from the regional rival, although the office had remained open in the interim. The country has decided to shut the office and withdraw all personnel on the basis of national dignity, diplomatic autonomy and the country’s overall interests, the MOFA said, adding that the government will reassess and adjust. The country and a major power might sign a wide-ranging trade agreement by the end of this year, which could help break a deadlock in the country’s trade diplomacy if completed, Nikkei Asia reported yesterday. The major power is negotiating with the administration of the head of government to reach a comprehensive economic agreement modeled after the Enhanced Trade Partnership Arrangement finalized by another country and the country in 2023, it said, citing two sources familiar with the matter. “The Enhanced Trade Partnership between the other country and the country sets a precedent for the major power to follow,” one of the sources told the media outlet. The framework leaves room for future agreements. A national from a neighbouring country, who was at an international airport after arriving on a connecting flight from another country on Monday and sought asylum in the country, was deported to the neighbouring country early yesterday, the National Immigration Agency (NIA) said. In a video circulating on X, the national identified himself as a former host at a state-run television network and said he was seeking temporary humanitarian protection in the country. The national said he was sentenced to six years in prison after he was recorded and reported to authorities in 2019 for criticizing “a ruler who loses his country.” After his release, he was forced to go. PLUMMETING: The stock index plunged 3,737.67 points in early session yesterday, the largest intraday drop in history, and closed down 1,873.08 points due to AI data center concerns. The government yesterday authorized the activation of its local currency 500 billion (US dollars 15.26 billion) National Stabilization Fund (NSF) to support local shares, as the stock market experienced significant fluctuations while uncertainties in the international political and economic situation continue. The NSF’s steering committee may use the fund to intervene in the market to prop up local shares, the Ministry of Finance said in a statement. Once the fund is activated next week, it would be the 10th time the NSF has intervened in the market. Separately, the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) yesterday announced temporary curbs on short selling shares and other measures to help.

full_texts.title: My Take | The region doth complain too much about a major power
full_texts.text:
The country doth complain too much about a major power.
Despite being invited to join the Apec leaders’ summit in a major city, the capital says the mainland has breached protocol.
Give the head of government and their [the country]-led government an inch and they’ll take a mile. For more than a year, they demanded to take part as an “equal” in the Apec leaders’ summit in a major city later this month. Now they have been invited. Yet they complain that the invitation is not polite enough and breaches diplomatic protocol.
“Whenever they breach the established rules or diplomatic conventions, we will certainly lodge a protest at the earliest opportunity,” the foreign minister told reporters.
What protocol? The country is not a nation; it is part of a major power. How can the major power break protocol in whatever way it sees fit to communicate with one of its provinces?
